title: Historiae Adversum Paganos
author: Paulus Orosius
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0215c.stoa001.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's CSEL.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: Anno ante urbem conditam MCLX confinem Arabiae regionem quae tunc Pentapolis uocabatur arsisse penitus igne caelesti inter alios etiam Cornelius Tacitus refert, qui sic ait:
passages.english: In the year 1160 before the founding of the City, the region bordering on Arabia which was then called Pentapolis was utterly burned by fire from heaven, as Cornelius Tacitus, among others, relates; he speaks as follows:

passages.original: fuisse autem absque Etruscis et Vmbris, quos astu Romani bello auocauerunt, Gallorum et Samnitium peditum CXL milia cccxxx, equitum uero XLVII milia Liuius refert, et carpentarios mille in armis contra aciem stetisse Romanam.
passages.english: Livy relates that, apart from the Etruscans and Umbrians, whom the Romans had cunningly drawn off by war, there were 140,330 foot soldiers of the Gauls and Samnites and 47,000 horsemen, and that a thousand wagon-fighters stood in arms against the Roman battle line.
passages.notes: 'carpentarios' is taken as men fighting from war-wagons (carpenta).

passages.original: Dixisse Aenean Virgilius refert, cum post pericula sua suorumque naufragia residuos aegre socios solaretur, Forsan et haec olim meminisse iuuabit.
passages.english: Virgil relates that Aeneas, when after his own dangers and the shipwrecks of his people he was consoling his surviving companions, who were in distress, said: "Perhaps one day it will be a pleasure to remember even these things."
passages.notes: 'aegre' could also go with 'solaretur' (he consoled them with difficulty).

passages.original: sed, ne qaemquam quasi temptatio cauillationis offendat, quod, cum Sibylla iratos deos dixerit, nos iram caelestem dixisse uideamur, audiat et intellegat, quia haec, etsi plerumque per aerias potestates fiunt, tamen sine arbitrio omnipotentis Dei omnino non fiunt.
passages.english: But so that no one may be offended, as if by an attempt at quibbling, because, when the Sibyl said the gods were angry, we seem to have spoken of heavenly anger, let him hear and understand that these things, even if they are mostly brought about through the powers of the air, nevertheless do not happen at all without the will of almighty God.

passages.original: uicti Мacedones castra amiserunt, VIII milia hostium eo die caesa, v milia capta Polybius scribit; Valerius dicit XL milia trucidata; Claudius uero XXXII milia interfecta commemorat.
passages.english: The Macedonians were defeated and lost their camp; Polybius writes that 8,000 of the enemy were slain that day and 5,000 captured; Valerius says 40,000 were slaughtered; Claudius, however, records 32,000 killed.

passages.original: Caesar Rubicone flumine transmeato, mox ut Ariminum uenit, quinque cohortes, quas tunc solas habebat, cum quibus, ut ait Liuius, orbem terrarum adortus est, quid facto opus esset, edocuit. deplorans iniurias suas, causam belli ciuilis, pro restituendis in patriam tribunis, esse testatus
passages.english: Caesar, having crossed the river Rubicon, as soon as he came to Ariminum, informed the five cohorts, which were all he had at that time and with which, as Livy says, he attacked the whole world, of what needed to be done. Lamenting the wrongs done to him, he declared that the cause of the civil war was the restoration of the tribunes to their homeland
passages.notes: The passage breaks off mid-sentence; 'esse testatus' seems to lack a following word (e.g. 'est').

passages.original: quod reuera bellum maximum et formidulosissimum quindecim legionibus per triennium gestum est, nec fere ullum maius bellum, sicut Suetonius adtestatur, post Punicum fuit.
passages.english: This war was indeed very great and most dreadful, waged with fifteen legions over three years, and there was hardly any greater war, as Suetonius attests, after the Punic [war].

passages.original: nam septingentesimo conditionis suae anno quattuordecim uicos eius incertum unde consurgens flamma consumpsit, nec umquam, ut ait Liuius, maiore incendio uastata est; adeo, ut post aliquot annos Caesar Augustus ad reparationem eorum, quae tunc exusta erant, magnam uim pecuniae ex aerario publico largitus sit.
passages.english: For in the seven hundredth year from its founding a fire, arising from no one knows where, consumed fourteen of its districts, and never, as Livy says, was it devastated by a greater conflagration; so much so that some years later Caesar Augustus granted a great sum of money from the public treasury for the restoration of what had then been burned.

passages.original: qui praeteriens ab Aegypto fines Palaestinae, apud Hierosolymam in templo Dei tunc sancto et celebri adorare contempsit, sicut Suetonius Tranquillus refert. quod Augustus ubi per eum conperit, prauo usus iudicio prudenter fecisse laudauit.
passages.english: He, passing from Egypt through the territory of Palestine, disdained to worship at Jerusalem in the temple of God, which was then holy and much frequented, as Suetonius Tranquillus relates. When Augustus learned of this from him, using a perverse judgement, he praised him for having acted wisely.

passages.original: Anno eiusdem nono expulsos per Claudium Vrbe Iudaeos losephus refert. sed me magis Suetonius mouet, qui ait hoc modo: Claudius Iudaeos inpulsore Christo adsidue tumultuantes Roma expulit;
passages.english: Josephus relates that in his ninth year the Jews were expelled from the City by Claudius. But Suetonius moves me more, who speaks as follows: "Claudius expelled from Rome the Jews, who were constantly rioting at the instigation of Christ;"

passages.original: itaque cum Iudaeos, multis eorum oppidis captis in urbem Hierosolymorum praecipue ob diem festum congregatos, obsidione clausisset, cognita Neronis morte hortatu plurimorum regum et ducum — maxime losepbi Iudaeorum ducis sententia, qui captus cum in uincla coiceretur, constantissime dixerat, sicut Suetonius refert, continuo se ab eodem sed imperatore soluendum — imperium adoptus est, relictoque in castris ad procurationem obsidionis Hierosolymorum filio Tito, per Alexandriam profectus est Romam; sed cognita interfectione Vitelli paulisper Alexandriae substitit.
passages.english: And so, when he had shut up the Jews under siege, after many of their towns had been taken, in the city of Jerusalem, where they had gathered chiefly on account of a feast day, on learning of Nero's death he obtained the imperial power at the urging of very many kings and commanders, and above all through the pronouncement of Josephus, the commander of the Jews, who, when he had been captured and was being thrown into chains, had declared most steadfastly, as Suetonius reports, that he would soon be released by the same man, but [then] as emperor. Leaving his son Titus in the camp to manage the siege of Jerusalem, he set out for Rome by way of Alexandria; but on learning of the killing of Vitellius he stayed for a short while at Alexandria.
passages.notes: 'losepbi' is a scanning error for 'Iosephi' (Josephus). 'adoptus' read as 'adeptus' (obtained).

passages.original: sexcenta milia Iudaeorum eo bello interfecta Cornelius et Suetonius referunt; Iosephus uero Iudaeus, qui ei tunc bello praefuit et apud Vespasianum propter praedictum imperium ueniam gratiamque meruerat, scribit undecies centena milia gladio et fame perisse, reliquias uero Iudaeorum diuersis actas condicionibus toto Orbe dispersas: quarum numerus ad nonaginta milia hominum fuisse narratur.
passages.english: Cornelius and Suetonius report that six hundred thousand Jews were killed in that war; but Josephus, a Jew, who at that time had commanded in that war and had earned pardon and favour with Vespasian because of his prediction of [his] imperial rule, writes that eleven hundred thousand perished by the sword and by famine, and that the remnants of the Jews, driven off under various conditions, were scattered over the whole world: their number is said to have been as many as ninety thousand people.
passages.notes: 'Cornelius' is presumably Cornelius Tacitus. 'ei ... bello' is read as 'eo bello' (that war).
